subtopic: MR. HOWARD (SKEENA)-ALLEGED FALSE ANSWER TO WRITTEN QUESTION
MR. HOWARD (SKEENA)-ALLEGED FALSE ANSWER TO WRITTEN QUESTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege regarding an answer given by the government to question No. 602, shown in Hansard at pages 2228 and 2229 for January 12, 1970. It came to my attention only this morning that it is a false answer and that, again, misleading information has been given to the House of Commons. Part of the question which was posed was:
Have all reclassified employees been retroactively paid the salary, allowances, pension and other benefits to which they were entitled as of the 1967 date-
And so on.
The answer given was "Yes". The fact of the matter, with regard to the one employee who at that time was involved in this situation, is that in fact he had only been paid retroactive salary and wages to December 1, 1968, and not to 1967, as had been asked and answered in the affirmative, and that he had been employed by the government in this capacity back on October 1, 1966.
There is another erroneous part of the answer which I shall not go into at this stage, but it deals with more than this one employee. The result of this false information is that the employee involved, a person of Indian descent, has been denied the further retroactive wages he should have received and that there may be involved another $2,000 or $3,000 in back wages. The erroneous answer to the other part of the question would involve at least 100 other caretakers of Indian day-schools, because likewise they have been denied their full benefit under the Public
Service Staff Relations Act and the wages which have accrued to them.
Based on this, Mr. Speaker, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), if you find there is a prima facie case of privilege:
That the Committee on Privileges and Elections be authorized to inquire into the information given by the government in response to question No. 602 as shown at pages 2228 and 2229 of Hansard for January 2, 1970, as well as into the matter of all persons employed by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development as Indian day-school caretakers.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. HOWARD (SKEENA)-ALLEGED FALSE ANSWER TO WRITTEN QUESTION
speechtext:
The hon. member for Skeena proposes that the House consider, by way of breach of parliamentary privilege, what he calls false information given in a return to a written question. I suggest to the hon. member that there are at least two procedural obstacles that he does not appear to have overcome in the presentation he has just made to the Chair and to the House. The first is that the Chair is not at liberty to rule that there is a prima facie case of privilege when the matter complained of is a dispute as to fact. There are many well known precedents which could be quoted in this respect.
The other difficulty relates to the requirement that the matter should be raised at the earliest opportunity. In this respect I refer hon. members to May's Seventeenth Edition, page 378, as follows:
The matter must be raised at the earliest opportunity. A matter of privilege which claims precedence over other public business should be a subject which has recently arisen.
As an example, the learned author makes the following statement:
A matter which occurred during the recess was refused precedence as a matter of privilege because it was not raised at the commencement of the session.
Similarly, a matter concerning an article in a newspaper published on 6 May was refused precedence because it was not raised till the 14th and a speech reported on a Saturday because it was not raised until the following Tuesday.
In the case brought before us we do not have a situation where the hon. member failed to raise the matter the day after the subject of privilege arose; it is, indeed, more than a year since this particular matter was reported in the Official Report of the proceedings of the House of Commons. I do not think it is sufficient for the hon. member to say that he has just become aware of the alleged inaccuracy of the return. It would be extremely difficult to find that the matter has, in fact, been raised at the first opportunity.
For these reasons I cannot agree with the hon. member that there is a prima facie case of privilege which ought to be considered by the House at this time.

This, Mr. Speaker, is my question of privilege. The Temporary Wheat Reserves Act provides for payments every year in which more than 178 million bushels of wheat are in storage, and payments would amount to more than $100 million if they were continued under that act. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. GLEAVE-ALLEGED MISLEADING STATEMENTS BY GOVERNMENT MEMBERS RESPECTING PAYMENTS UNDER TEMPORARY WHEAT RESERVES ACT
speechtext:
The hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar has given the required notice of his intention to raise this matter by way of a question of privilege. I, of course, do not intend to consider the matter lightly because I realize the importance of the situation and the interest of all hon. members in this very important and obviously contentious issue.
The hon. member suggests that there is a breach of parliamentary privilege, either a breach of his privileges or of those of the House, in that, to use his words, "the Canadian government by statements outside the House is misleading the public." I cannot judge whether that is so or not, but I suggest to the hon. member that this cannot possibly be the basis for the submission of a question of privilege.
I have gone into the precedents and considered the Standing Order at length yesterday when a similar motion was proposed which, I might say, was in all points similar to that proposed today by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar. There is no point in restating the precedents I referred to yesterday. I am sure the hon. member will appreciate that in view of the precedents I quoted yesterday and the citations mentioned in my ruling I cannot rule today, contrary to my ruling yesterday, that there is a prima facie case of privilege.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to move a motion pursuant to Standing Order 43. I believe unanimous consent is required. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 26 and ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the declaration by a United States official that the safeguards for Canada in the Canada-U.S. auto pact must be dropped before the U.S. import surcharge can be withdrawn and the implications of this U.S. position for an industry already experiencing serious lay-offs.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext:
The hon. member for Brant has given due notice of his intention to move this motion under Standing Order 26. Meanwhile I have had an opportunity to give careful and sympathetic study to the request outlined in the motion proposed by the hon. member.
The Chair does appreciate the seriousness of the matter raised by the hon. member. It is undoubtedly one which is
Questions

September 29, 1971
of national interest and of concern to all hon. members. In determining whether the business of the House ought to be set aside for the purpose of considering such an important and urgent situation, the Chair has to be guided by certain criteria specified in Standing Order 26. One of these requirements is that the matter proposed for discussion should relate to an emergency which calls for immediate and urgent consideration by the House. In other words, it is not only urgency of the matter which has to be considered but the urgency of debate.
While I surmise that the House would want an opportunity to discuss this problem, I doubt that the urgency of the situation would require that the debate be held today or tomorrow rather than later. speechtext:

"3. (3) Notwithstanding subsection (1), the allowance payable under this section to a veteran, widow or orphan may be paid to that veteran, widow or orphan who absents himself from Canada after the coming into force of this Act if, on the day that he leaves Canada, he

speechtext:
As I was saying, one need only look at the Douglas Aircraft Corporation in Mississauga, in my riding, which employs 6,000 to 8,000 men to make aircraft wings for assembly in California. This firm has been absorbing the shipping costs, and since the change resulting from floating the Canadian dollar it has had to absorb the difference in dollar value and still compete with its counterparts in the United States.
The surcharge will cost this firm about $165,000 a week, less any assistance it may receive under the unemployment support bill. If labour causes an additional disadvantage, is it not obvious that this company may well accept United States governmental persuasion to repatriate to the United States at a location much closer to California and in a state offering financial assistance? Should we encourage this firm to leave, or encourage it to stay? If this firm moves, the resulting loss of jobs in Canada would number about 10,000.
We have also heard of the proposed Domestic International Sales Corporation, commonly called DISC, which would seek to lure firms like the Douglas Corporation back to the United States by offering home-based corporations tremendous advantages over foreign-based ones and by allowing tax deferral for earnings on export sales. Many think we in Canada export only pulp, oil and wheat, but that is not so. Half of our manufactured goods are exported, the majority of them to the United States. The U.S. surcharge was not meant to affect their imports of our raw materials because they need them but, rather, the export of our manufactured or high labour content goods. In the long run we must work out a set of rules with the United States authorities which will give our manufacturing concerns an equal opportunity with the American firms, or we shall revert to being an agricultural nation living on our natural resources because we will not have the money with which to manufacture and trade.
None of the measures I have mentioned is pleasing, but the worst one, a real sleeper, has received very little attention in public discussions so far. It is the 10 per cent tax credit on the cost of all new machinery and equipment produced in and for use in the United States. This is called by the innocuous name "job development tax credit." But look at what it does. The 10 per cent tax credit on

all new machinery purchased in the United States for use there, along with the usual tax write off would amount to a price reduction of 12 per cent to 14 per cent for at least a year, and something less than that for an indefinite period.
The expressed long-term purpose of this tax benefit is, first, to cause replacement of productive facilities with new, modern equipment with the newest technological innovations and thus increase the productivity of their workers and, second, to thus make their domestic industries more competitive in domestic and foreign markets. Third, this in turn would supply more jobs, provide a sound basis for future wage increases where productivity has increased, and decrease inflationary pressures on prices. This means that no United States industry would buy a piece of machinery or mechanical equipment in Canada if it or a substitute can be made in the United States. Last year we exported about $332 million worth of machinery and mechanical equipment to tne United States. If nothing is done to replace these sales we will lose 20,000 skilled and semi-skilled jobs almost immediately, and about 50 per cent of them in Quebec where we were trying so hard to create employment through regional development.
This is not all. United States firms extract perhaps 70 per cent of our natural resources. This part of the operation being low in labour content, we naturally hope and try to persuade them to process the raw materials to some extent in Canada. But if a new mine or other natural resource is started here now, there is no way that an American or Canadian would buy new machinery here to process the raw material in Canada. He would be disadvantaged in the machinery purchase. After extracting the raw material he must process it in the United States for this advantage and other benefits which the United States is innovating to encourage and aid industry and, thus, the creation of jobs. The result is, if we do nothing about this measure we are in effect allowing United States citizens here, Canadians and all others, to be forced to process our raw materials in the United States.
And now the most jolting realization of all. The United States will give this huge tax credit, with resulting loss of revenue, so that all of their industry will take advantage of it and quickly introduce all technological improvements available and thus become more efficient and productive in every type of industry. They give business a year under the full 10 per cent incentive, so one may be reasonably certain that all steps possible to introduce new and more efficient machinery will be taken quickly. This will not affect the machinery and mechanical business only but the whole manufacturing industry. In all business, industrial and commercial, carried on by Canadians we will be seriously disadvantaged on the U.S. market and against Americans in the other marketplaces of the world because the American competitor has, by tax incentive, been assisted in modernizing his equipment up to the moment.
We cannot afford to allow this situation to stand another day. We must undertake to introduce legislation in the form of an amendment to the bill, retroactive to this date, to give exactly the same advantages to industry purchas-
September 29, 1971

ing Canadian machinery and mechanized equipment for use in Canada and to further improve the whole industrial climate by taxation and other incentives and the removal of annoying and unnecessary obstacles.
During the last year we imported about $1,325 million worth of machinery and mechnical equipment. This is about four times the amount we exported. From my conversations with representatives of industry I am satisfied that we could produce in Canada $660 million worth of that which we have been importing. With the amendment to this bill which I propose we could increase sales in Canada by that amount, about $660 million, thus avoiding the loss of 20,000 jobs and in fact creating an extra 30,000 jobs. Moreover, such a provision would cause us to look to ourselves as Canadians and reexamine whether at this time of emergency we could not somehow find the product available in Canada.
From my contacts with industry I am satisfied that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is doing an excellent job. But what about some of the other departments? Under the proposed Canada Labour Code Bill C-253, if an industrialist proposed a technological change that might make him more efficient by introducing a machine which would do the work of six people, he must give notice of the change to the bargaining agent of the union, along with considerable detail as required by the act and as may be further required by the regulations under the act.
If the bargaining agent makes certain allegations there must be a hearing before the board. The board can direct the employer not to proceed and has considerable other power to throw blocks and even prevent the technological change no matter how much more competitive it might have made that industry in the world market. On the face of it one might think that this proposal is kind to labour. But this is not so. It is this type of thinking that has made our railways so overstructured in labour content and so costly, and thus destructive of the efficient movement and lower price of goods which would make them more competitive.
The new competition act, Bill C-256, which in a sense contemplates confrontations between government and industry, or at least provides for overly severe policing, is in a very real sense a form of nuisance and in fact has been used to prosecute and harass on charges that are old and really quite trivial. I suggest that more effort should be diverted to encouraging, rather than hindering, industry.
When the United States authorities introduced a wage freeze and it was suggested that this action would prevent an increase in wages at Douglas Aircraft in Canada, what a fuss was raised by the NDP, and one of our ministers said the United States action could not influence our wages. It would have been better had we all reassured business that we have enough intelligence to realize that if wages in Canada go beyond those of competing industry in the United States, where productivity is the same or higher, our industry is disadvantaged to the point where it will eventually have to close shop. One wonders what international labour, under their United States leaders, is trying to do. With a freeze on wages in the aircraft industry in the United States, a strike at the Canadian plant which provides the wings for the planes would be an
Income Tax Act
indirect strike in the United States. If this plant could thus tie up the whole United States aircraft industry, certainly it would be transferred back to the United States. Surely we must realize that the time has come, when we are faced with these new United States protective measures, that we must encourage industry and co-operate with industry because otherwise the jobs which we must have will not be saved.
Japan and the United States encourage, encourage and encourage industry. It seems in Canada that we give the impression that we want more and more from industry and that we want to give more and more by way of handouts to other people whose only retort is, "Is that all you are going to give me?"
I have heard it said so often in this House that we should tax profit more, put greater taxes on big business. The profits that are not taken in taxes are distributed in dividends, and the dividends in Canadian big business are not high. In fact, they are so low that people will not buy shares in existing companies or new companies which would create jobs. If the profits are low and dividends are low, in no way can we find the money to create extra jobs.
We must react with more positive and speedier action, not only because it is necessary to avoid massive loss of employment but we must appear determined to keep the economy healthy so that investment and expansion will not draw back again and American capital leave to return to the United States, and Canadian capital migrate out of Canada to other countries. If our machinery and mechanical industry were given the same tax credit advantage as in the United States, the American corporations which have been exporting these goods into Canada would be in trouble, naturally. Then we would have a strong American lobby assisting us in our quest for more reasonable trade arrangements between Canada and the U.S.-a very helpful ally, I would think.
If we wait until the Americans are satisfied with their trade balance we will lose some of those industries which began specializing or, as they call it, rationalizing two or three years ago. By the time we return to the former trade pattern those industries will have lost many of their customers, much of their skilled labour and their ability to compete against their larger competitors. Under the American DISC plan many American companies will be persuaded to take their export production back to the United States and perhaps also their whole production. In some cases Canadian manufacturers will be asked to fill in those gaps for Canadian consumption. This is another reason for a tax incentive on the purchase of Canadian machinery, so that Canadians will take the gamble and buy new machinery to replace this production and to re-employ labour where jobs have been lost.
In conclusion, I say that although such an amendment would indeed be helpful and it is absolutely essential as an immediate step, we must still bring forth more concrete and substantial incentives for Canadian-owned companies to export. If our resources are to be sold, they should not be sold just for dollars, but for jobs. Our resources will have to be exported in the finished form or alternatively an equivalent number of jobs created by an

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-259, commonly referred to as the tax reform bill of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) because, coming from an agricultural riding, I find that unfortunately it spells bad news for our farmers. This naturally means that I and other hon. members and colleagues should raise our voices in protest where we feel injustices are being meted out. Just to refresh our memory I would read the amendment that is before the House. It was moved on September 13 by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and is as follows:
That this House deeply concerned with unacceptable levels of inflation, persisting unemployment and stagnant industry and conscious of the necessity for meaningful tax reform declines to give second reading to a bill which does not provide sufficient stimulus to the economy of Canada with appropriate tax cuts and incentives, does not contain adequate tax exemptions and is not calculated to materially improve business and labour conditions in Canada now or in the foreseeable future.
Of course, the terms of this bill, as with any other taxing measure, not only affects our farmers but also our fishermen, small business, the labouring man and all other sectors of our economy. In fact, when the government refers to Bill C-259 as tax reform legislation I have grave doubts about the correctness of their terminology. It appears to me to have finally emerged as a subtle plan to gouge more and higher taxes out of more and more Canadians who are already staggering under the burden, which is having the effect of an economic millstone around our necks in our endeavour to produce goods at a price that will compete on world markets and provide for our basic, everyday needs.
The original Carter commission report on taxation, brought in several years ago for the government's consideration, did contain a number of suggested tax reforms, but it was so socialistic in many areas that even the NDP, then led by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), had to back away from several sections of the report, although at first blush he and his party seemed to be ready to clasp to their bosoms the whole program as outlined.
The white paper of the Minister of Finance was a well watered-down version of the Carter report, and today we are looking at a bill that, again, is only a shadow of his original intentions planned for us in the white paper which was so much debated a year ago. This change of heart can be credited chiefly to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), who almost in a one-man crusade across this country last spring and summer alerted thousands of Canadians in all walks of life to just what the white paper on taxation would do to them and to our economy in general if it were thrust on us in its original form.
In the present bill, everyone is in agreement with increasing tax exemptions for those in the low-income brackets. Every one of us also supports the closing of loopholes in our tax laws with respect to income tax evasion, and perhaps we are in agreement with several other sections of the bill, depending where we sit in this House. However, in my opinion these suitable and neces-

sary changes could have been made by simple amendments to the present law without all the political fanfare, a wasteful spending of the taxpayers' dollars and the consequent subterfuge leading people to believe that great changes were taking place when in fact they were being asked to dig up more tax dollars for this spendthrift government.
I do not pretend to be a tax expert, but if what I read and hear is true, this bill in its present form will lead to the greatest tax jungle in Canadian history. It seems that our top accountants and tax lawyers who have looked at the bill are about ready to throw up their hands in despair when it comes to properly interpreting the proposed legislation. If this is the case with the so-called tax experts, imagine the trouble and feeling of despair of the ordinary layman when he looks at how he may be affected by this legislation.
At this point I wish to deal with two aspects of the finance minister's tax reform bill, how it will affect the agricultural industry, farmers in particular, and how it will affect co-operatives, a matter with which some hon. members are probably involved. First of all, let us consider the farmers. Under the present law a farmer may classify a group of animals as his basic herd, and gains and losses are treated as capital gains and capital losses and are tax exempt. However, under the new tax reform bill, the basic herd provision and straight line depreciation will be phased out. Livestock farmers will be able to establish a basic herd as of December 31, 1971, and any gain thereon will be tax free, but no additions to the basic herd may be made after December 31. When livestock is sold after December 31, 1971, the sale will be considered as going out of the basic herd or the other herd and will be subject to special rules.
Assets acquired after December 31, 1971, must be depreciated on the diminishing balance system. If proceeds from the sale of assets, depreciated on a straight line basis, exceed their cost or valuation day value, the excess is capital gain. As an example, trading-in tractors and combines for new machinery will be affected in this respect. Under the new legislation capital gain will be subject to taxation. As far as a hobby farmer is concerned, he may still deduct only $5,000 of his annual farming loss from other income. But in addition, any amount of interest and property taxes not deducted because of this limitation may be applied to reduce any proceeds on the eventual sale of the farm.
In general, income gained from farming and fishing will be brought more into line with the tax treatment of other businesses. Farmers probably will be taxed somewhat more heavily in this area, but it is impossible to say how much because the government has not calculated additional revenues which might result in this area. One measure in the tax reform bill that will adversely affect farmers is that no new additions and sales can be deducted after the livestock farmer has established his basic herd as of December 31, 1971.
Another part of this bill that will spell bad news for farmers is valuation day, because property will be subject to the new capital gains tax proposed in the bill. This capital gains tax is new to Canada and will begin with
September 29, 1971

valuation day. Some people may not be familiar with the term "valuation day" or V-day as it is commonly called. Some time before the new tax plan takes effect the government will declare what it calls valuation day. Only the gains realized after that date will be taxed. If a capital asset is valued at below cost on that date, the cost value will be taken as the starting figure for the system. For many farmers this measure will not mean much, but farmers who sell to developers will face a large tax bill.
Under the new plan there will be no capital gains tax on a taxpayer's principal residence, and one acre of surrounding land will also be exempted. That is to say, no capital gain will be calculated when he sells his acre of land or his house, but his farm machinery and barn are still subject to capital gains. However, this plan could hardly bring any comfort to farmers who have considerably more than one acre of land, so farmers will have an alternative. A farmer may choose the white paper formula for a $1,000 annual deduction against gains on his farmhouse and all his farm property, whichever plan is more beneficial to him.
One aspect of the finance minister's capital gains tax structure which does not make sense is this: if all capital gains are to be taxed, why aren't all capital losses to be deducted? Mr. I. H. Asper, in the Globe and Mail of July 1, 1971, clarified this situation very well as follows:
Take, for example, the situation of the farmer who, because his children do not want to carry on the family farm, sells his assets. He has a capital gain of, for example, $50,000 which is taxed.
He retires and invests all of his money in the market. Three or four years later he liquidates because his investments are not advancing, and suffers a $50,000 loss.
In fairness he should not pay any tax because he is even, not ahead-he has had a taxable $50,000 gain and a non-deductible $50,000 loss.
Now if another farmer had the same results but in reverse order-first a $50,000 capital loss and then later made a $50,000 capital gain, the gain would not be taxed because the law, as written, provides that a loss can be carried forward indefinitely to offset future gains. But the reverse is not true, resulting in an unequitable situation.
At first the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool appeared to be one of the few organizations throughout the tax reform debate that was ready to support partially some of the finance minister's proposals, for the simple reason that they thought Saskatchewan farmers would likely be among the first to benefit from measures to reduce taxes for some and eliminate them entirely for others. However, the pool has many qualifications. For example, Mr. Speaker, it has argued that a tax on capital gains may hit farmers and other small businessmen particularly hard because most of them seek to retire on proceeds from the sale of their farm or business and fear the proceeds may be whittled away by a collection of tax on the capital gain. The pool has said that farmers and small businessmen should be permitted to purchase a registered retirement plan from the proceeds of the sale of their business before a capital gains tax is levied. But the minister's tax reform legislation does not appear to allow opportunity for this kind of purchase.
Let us now consider the new tax bill as it affects cooperatives and credit unions. In a rather obscure and complicated way the bill seems intent upon profoundly altering the nature and goals of co-operatives in Canada.
Income Tax Act
Under the present law, new co-operatives are exempt from taxation for the first three years. The new bill proposes to withdraw this three-year tax exemption.
Consumer patronage dividends are to remain exempt as long as they can be distributed. Under the present law, patronage dividends on production goods, for example farm supplies, are considered a reduction of cost and must be taken into income by the recipient and are taxable at the recipient's personal rate. Patronage dividends for production goods will remain as income under the new bill.
The capital employed principle has been drastically changed under the new bill. Whereas now co-operatives cannot reduce their taxable income below 3 per cent of the capital employed, the formula for calculating the capital employed under the new tax reform bill will include essentially only members' equity, that is, shares, loans and general reserves, and the rate has been increased to 5 per cent. The only deduction is the interest paid on members' loans.
These changes will have the accumulated effect that less and less of a co-operative's earnings can be distributed as patronage dividends on purchases. This means that the earnings of co-operatives will gradually have to be distributed on the basis of the equity owned by the members. This will force co-operatives into the pattern of investor-owned corporations rather than service corporations distributing earnings on the basis of use. When this point is reached, co-ops would be better to incorporate as ordinary corporations because then the shares would not be on call. It is unbelievable that the government of Canada wants to kill the co-op system in this way.
The tax on employed capital wfes introduced in the amendments to the Income Tax Act of 1948 purely as a political answer to opponents of co-operatives, and was not suggested or recommended by any of the various royal commissions which inquired into the position of co-operatives. It is an inequitable tax, practised nowhere else in the world. Some years ago the Danish government attempted this method but soon abandoned it.
It should be kept in mind that earnings on non-member business and money put into reserves or held by the co-operative itself are taxed at normal corporation rates. No one questions these regulations. The Minister of Finance has indicated that he will be receptive to amendments in this area. We hope he follows through on his word, and we intend to press the government to explain just what it means by these changes. Special sectors of the economy, for example the resource industries and small businesses, have received favourable consideration in the tax reform bill to assure their continued viability, and we feel co-operatives should receive similar treatment. These new tax reform proposals appear to favour the distribution of co-operative earnings as interest on members' equity rather than as patronage refunds. Perhaps the members of co-operatives, and not the federal finance department, should determine how earnings of co-operatives are allocated to members who are also patrons.
Aside from the tax reform bill there are two items in the minister's June budget which also affect the agricultural sector-the end of the federal estate tax and the elimination of the 12 per cent tax on margarine. Roy Atkinson,
8288
Income Tax Act

September 29, 1971
president of the National Farmers Union, has said that the imposition of the capital gains tax will nullify any benefits that could come from the abolition of the estate tax. The National Farmers Union has been advocating an end to the estate tax for some time. However, this tax was never one of the biggest problems facing farmers, particularly in western Canada. George Heffelfinger, president of the National Grain Company, was much more optimistic about the effect of this particular portion of the budget. He said that the estate tax in the past has been responsible for the sale of many small businesses and farms, particularly to American buyers.
The elimination of the 12 per cent tax on margarine has drawn varied reaction from within the dairy industry which stands to be hardest hit by a projected lowering of the price of margarine. Philip Isaacs, former manager of the Winnipeg Dairy and Poultry Co-operative, is reported as saying that the dairy processing industry has been urging the removal of this tax for several years. He said he did not expect any great increase in the consumption of margarine, but conceded it may cause many difficulties for dairy producers. The dairy farmers of Canada, on the other hand, have been opposing the removal of this tax. Roy Atkinson has said the removal of this tax may make margarine more competitive with butter and may pose a problem for the butter producers.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, on the basis of the serious reservations expressed by my colleagues earlier in the debate on Bill C-259 and in light of the views I have just expressed, I have no alternative but to support the amendment now before the House.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the events leading to the introduction of Bill C-259 were billed as an exercise in participatory democracy. That is how it was publicized. To those hon. members who may be under the delusion that this is what took place, I suggest that it was one giant fizzle. We did not have participatory democracy in any way, shape or form. This is demonstrated most vividly in the result of the exercise as expressed in the form of Bill C-259 now before us. It in no way speaks for the people of Canada nor does it relate to the needs and desires of many people throughout the country.
Perhaps we should ask ourselves who won the exercise, such as it was. I think this was demonstrated in the concessions made by the government with respect to capital gains, to the mining, oil and gas industries, the difference in the way various forms of income are treated and the difference in the treatment of working people compared to businessmen and others who receive their income in different forms.
Mr. Speaker, if there is any thought in the minds of members opposite that the bill now before us is an expression of the just society, they had better think again. As soon as they have looked beyond the few goodies contained in the bill, people will realize that in fact it contains a great many inequities. The public will react to the hoax that has been perpetrated upon them and this will result in a further build-up of pressure in our society for some sort of meaningful change. It will be realized that the

government of the day has not been responsive to the very real needs and desires of the people.
I should like to deal with some aspects of the debate that has taken place on this bill, Mr. Speaker. First of all, I should like to deal with the argument that has been debated very widely on the whole question of equity versus growth. It has been quite apparent that the primary consideration of members on the government side of the House, in many instances, and on the part of the government itself has been in terms of giving more emphasis and more priority to growth considerations. This has been the justification put forward for some of the measures proposed in this bill.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if they really want to examine this question in depth it will be apparent that it is not possible to have true and meaningful growth unless it is linked with considerations of equity and unless equity is built into the tax system in all respects. Before we can have any real tax reform we must have more emphasis on tax equity than so far has been demonstrated in this bill.
I acknowledge that one important departure which the government has proposed is the introduction of a capital gains tax. It is a half-baked measure but it does give some hope for the future. Once the breakthrough is made in terms of introducing the principle of taxation on capital gains, it may be possible in the future to introduce further improvements in order to realize a greater degree of equity.
Looking at the over-all picture, I think one of the worst features of the bill is the manner in which it deals with the resource industries, particularly mining, oil and gas. It continues a system of concessions made available to those industries which is not available to any other sector or taxpayer in the Canadian economy. This seems to me to result in a very serious distortion of our economic system and of the pattern of our economic activity. It will result in greater incentives and greater inducements to development within that sector of the economy, but that is not necessarily the best allocation of resources in terms of our development policy. It will not necessarily result in the greatest possible number of jobs. It is well known that these primary industries have a very low labour input. They do have a high capital input and on many occasions in the past it has been necessary for Canada to import the capital required to bring about the development of these industries, but in terms of new jobs the result has been minimal.
There has been added pressure on the Canadian dollar and on our international economic position by way of added inflows of capital. The additional export of raw material has not produced much benefit. It is probably true that as a result of the concessions contained in this legislation and in the government's policy there are some marginal mining operations which have benefited, but I suggest that the allocation of resources to those industries which results from the influence of our tax system is not in the best interests of Canada. The suggestion that a change in the present system will result in a massive outflow of capital and resources industries is straight nonsense, Mr. Speaker. Certainly, these industries will make a noise and will protest. But I think when we see the end result we will realize that only very marginal industries are affected in any way.
September 29, 1971

Income Tax Act
It seems to me that we must keep these factors in mind when thinking of the current economic crisis facing Canada as a result of President Nixon's new economic measures. The fact is that the Canadian dollar is under severe pressure at present. In large part, but not totally, this has been brought about by our heavy emphasis on primary, non-renewable resource industries. These industries export most of their products in a raw or semi-processed form, the result being a heavy inflow of United States dollars to Canada. At the same time this produces little in the way of benefits for Canadians.
In my contribution to the debate this afternoon I should like to deal with one particular problem at some length. It is of a serious nature. I want to deal with the proposals in this bill with respect to taxation of co-operatives and credit unions. I feel that this constitutes a very serious problem. It has been brought to the attention of all members of this House. I am pleased to note that some members of all political parties have expressed concern about this matter. This shows, I think, that something has gone wrong with the system responsible for the introduction of this bill.
It seems that either nobody in the Department of Finance really understands what the co-operative movement is about-and I can hardly believe that since many capable and competent people are in the employ of the department-or somewhere along the line, before the bill was finalized in its present form, somebody got to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) or to the government and brought undue influence to bear. That has resulted in the atrocious proposals we have before us in clauses 135, 136 and 137. I do not hesitate in saying that from the viewpoint of the co-operative and credit union movements the proposals in this bill which affect them are nothing short of disastrous.
I think all hon. members should pause and think about this matter before they pass lightly over the proposals introduced by the government. We must keep in mind the history of the credit union and co-operative movements and the contribution they have made to Canadian society and to the economy. These movements are dedicated to helping people and to enabling people to exercise a greater degree of control over their own affairs. Their operations have been built largely on the principle of self-help. They have arisen in large measure because of the very real needs of Canadian people in many walks of life-not just in one sector of the economy, in one sector of our society or in one geographic area. In all the areas of Canadian society we have seen the credit union and cooperative movements grow in response to the needs of people and their desire to help themselves, to improve their conditions, their community and their country.
If the government is to take the step of doing something that actually will destroy the co-operative and credit union movements-and I suggest that is what is at stake- I suggest it will be perpetrating on this country one of the most serious follies we have witnessed in a long time. I also suggest that the co-operative and credit union movements have made a great contribution to Canada in terms of bringing about a greater degree of equality within our society and of bringing somewhat closer than would
otherwise be the case equality of opportunity and equality of condition. If we are to think of the future of Canada in meaningful terms, we must think about these matters.
If the government continues on a course which results in the destruction of the co-operative and credit union movements in Canada, I suggest it will be taking a major step toward destroying Canadian society and democracy. Our co-operative movement is dedicated to the principle of democracy. It is thoroughly steeped in the principle of democracy. It is an expression of democracy in its truest form in social, economic and political terms. For these reasons I suggest that the government must reconsider the proposals contained in this bill.
I think we must look at clauses 135, 136 and 137 of this bill, Mr. Speaker, and ask ourselves this question: What will happen to a society that cannot tolerate a different form of organizing its affairs than that which seems to predominate? We must also ask ourselves: Are we to have a tax system that is designed primarily to meet the needs of people, that is designed primarily in terms of people, or are we to have a tax system that thinks first in terms of money and capital? I think the answer is obvious when we consider that simple proposition.
We must translate that proposition into real terms with respect to the legislation now before us. I believe that the legislation as drafted thinks first in terms of money and capital. Those who drafted it and decided on the form in which it would be introduced, it seems to me, thought only of some form of economic structure or organization which begins with capital and financial considerations. They did not begin from the basic premise which is: Before you have money, before you have capital in any form you must have people, and it is people who are the prime movers in society and in our economy.
Members of my party, Mr. Speaker, have often been accused of being doctrinaire in their approach to our economy. It seems to me that clauses 135, 136 and 137 constitute one of the best examples of a doctrinaire approach ever envisaged. It seems that those responsible for including these clauses in the bill could think only in terms of classical capitalism. They could think only in terms of some form of economic organization which begins with a capital structure based on a classical capitalist type of economic organization. I suggest seriously to the government that a society which cannot accommodate a variety of approaches involving social and economic considerations is doomed. The minister must consider that when approaching this question.
Under the co-operative movement people have banded together to deal with their own problems. They wanted to help themselves. That was the prime, motivating force behind the co-operative and credit union movements. I suggest that these movements have developed a unique form of organization, a unique type of corporate structure, you might say, which differs from the usual type of corporate structure in our economy. The government has totally failed to take into account in the bill before us the unique characteristics of the movement.
I assure those on the other side of the House, the government in particular, that many of us will not stand idly by and see the co-operative and credit union movements

September 29, 1971
Income Tax Act
destroyed. We will stand in this House and fight for the changes that are necessary in order to produce a fair deal for this movement. I serve notice on the government that many of us will do battle when we come to these clauses of the bill. The operation and the structure of the co-operative and credit union movements differ in some respects, although they are based on similar principles. I would like to deal with each in turn because I believe there are some considerations that must be brought to the attention of the House.
Members will be familiar with representations that have been made to them by both the co-operative movement and the credit union movement. The credit union movement has expressed some very real and valid concerns with regard to the proposals in Bill C-259. We have to keep in mind that Bill C-259 proposes, for the first time, to remove the present exemption from taxation of caisses populaires and credit unions. This is a new departure in the Canadian tax scene. The last major change in this area was in the late 1940s. At that time the McDougall royal commission studied the question of taxation of cooperatives and credit unions. In spite of the changes and recommendations they made with regard to co-operatives, they recommended that credit unions should not be subject to taxation. I quote from the McDougall commission report:
Credit unions provide a method whereby people in poor circumstances are encouraged to develop a habit of thrift, since by pooling their savings they can provide a source of credit for themselves in time of need.
That only has to do with the question of taxing credit unions as such, taxing their surpluses or net income. I think it is fair to say that the credit union movement has very serious concerns about regard to the manner in which taxation will be imposed on them. I would like to enumerate some of their major concerns. First, members of the credit union and caisse populaire movement request an equality of tax with that accorded to corporations and the availability to corporations of a lower tax rate of 25 per cent. Of course, private corporations can under the revised rules continue the application to them of a lower rate of tax by the payment of dividends.
It must also be kept in mind that under provincial laws governing the operation of caisses populaires and credit unions, reserves set up by a caisse populaire or credit union cannot be distributed to members to provide for the continuation of a lower rate of tax as provided in other sectors of the tax system. Credit unions and caisses populaires ask that modified rules be provided for them so that the period during which they have received the reduced rate of tax of 25 per cent is extended in a manner equitable to that provided for corporations.
The second major point raised by the credit union movement is that payments made by a credit union or caisse populaire as a payment of interest or dividends, as they are commonly known, on members' shares, are not deductible as an expense. That is the proposal in the bill. This provision demonstrates a failure to recognize that the shares of a credit union or caisse populaire are a form of deposit by their members and are not shares similar in nature to ordinary corporate shares such as hon. members opposite are generally familiar with.

The third major concern is that clause 137 imposes very severe limitations on the manner in which a credit union or caisse populaire may carry on its business or in the manner in which it may invest its funds. I feel this question has to be looked at as well. They are also concerned about some of the transitional provisions developed for credit unions and caisses populaires in the application of Bill C-259.
Finally, members of caisses populaires object to the principle of "capital employed" limiting the patronage refunds that may be made by a credit union or caisse populaire to reduce the cost of borrowing by their members. This is a very reasonable set of objections which must be taken into account by the government. The National Association of Canadian Credit Unions and several other credit union and caisse populaire organizations made these representations to the government. They are also making them to members of the House of Commons. I think it is incumbent upon every member of this House to give them very serious consideration.
Members must bear in mind that the credit union movement has been of very great service to thousands of people across Canada in providing a start for them in solving their financial problems and financing the necessities of life. It is recognized that there is now general acceptance of the value and role of credit unions across Canada. It must be kept in mind that the people who invest their savings in credit unions are subject to different levels of taxation. No one is quarrelling with the principle that the dividends received from savings in credit unions, which are termed as shares, should be subject to taxation at whatever level may apply to the individual. It must be emphasized that there is a very serious malaise in our economy and our society if it is not possible to find a way of accommodating our tax system to the very unique structure and role that is played by this movement.
I would like to deal with the situation of the co-operative movement because it plays a very important role in the Canadian scene. The latest figures show that there are
1,700,000	members of co-operatives across Canada. Many are small community organizations but there are also large operations. These organizations have very real concerns which I believe should be made known to members of this House.
Co-operatives in general object most strenuously to the "capital employed" concept contained in Bill C-259. This substantially reduces the amount of patronage refunds which can be paid to members. Second, reducing patronage refunds hits at the economic existence of co-operatives. This point relates to my earlier submission that it will result in the destruction of some co-operatives and in other cases will seriously hamper their growth. It has to be kept in mind that patronage refunds are part of the investment required to enable a co-operative to operate. If a co-operative has no means of raising equity capital except through the reinvestment of patronage refunds in its share structure, it is obviously unable to expand and develop. This is the practice followed by many co-operatives-they do plow back patronage refunds into their capital structure. This provides them with the resources necessary to continue their operations and expand them if desired.
September 29, 1971

There are other objections which need to be taken into account. I was very much concerned by a statement made earlier by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) when he led off the debate on behalf of the Progressive Conservative party. He made some comments with regard to the taxation of co-operatives. I quote from his speech as reported in Hansard at page 7762 for September 13:
We have had quite a reaction to this bill from the co-ops. I do not know what the House is going to decide, but it seems to me that the government has advanced its proposals after looking at some of the largest co-ops in the country, organizations which have lost their co-operative origins, that operate in the hundreds of millions of dollars class, their boards of directors being far removed from the ordinary members, in the same way as the boards of the biggest multinational corporations are far removed from the shareholders.
Unfortunately the government's proposals gather up into the same net hundreds if not thousands of small local co-operatives. I am speaking of co-operatives organized on a local self-help basis.
There is no question but that this statement reflects a serious lack of understanding of the nature of the co-operative movement. It is certainly true that many large cooperatives operate on a large scale. There are many others which operate simply on the basis of serving a small local community. But I suggest that all of them are part and parcel of the co-operative movement. I do not say the co-operative movement is free from criticism with respect to the extent to which it has kept contact with its membership, but this is something which ought to be dealt with within the movement itself.
If you take time to look at some of the large co-operatives in Canada you will find that many of them have made monumental efforts to keep in contact with their members. It seems the hon. member is not familiar with the efforts of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, for example, to keep in touch with its membership and carry out an on-going program of membership participation in its activities and in the decision-making process. I invite him to take a close look at the highly developed organization, structure and pattern of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. I think it is a first-class example of the way in which organizations could keep in closer touch with their membership.
I think the hon. member for Edmonton West was off-base when he suggested that the tax proposals contained in clauses 135 and 137 were designed primarily with the very large co-operatives in mind. In fact, some of the very large co-ops will be hit most severely. Many of the large co-operatives are now being called upon to undertake expansion programs in order to meet new conditions and will be unable to continue in existence if the bill now before us is enacted.
Hon. members will be familiar with the representations which have been made by the movement to the Minister of Finance. The co-op movement has objected to the continuation of the capital employed concept as contained in Bill C-259. I should like to pose to the government the same question as the co-operative movement has posed: What is the rationale behind the capital employed concept? Is there any rational explanation for using a fixed capital employed concept? What justification is there for doing so?
Income Tax Act
Having set an arbitrary level in a capital employed formula-it was 3 per cent as applied to co-operatives under the old act; the percentage is now to be raised to 5 per cent-the principle is to be extended to the credit union movement. The co-operatives find the emphasis placed on the relation between income and capital to be unreasonable and illogical. They view this as a form of discrimination and point out that no similar provision appears in the proposed tax bill affecting other methods of doing business.
There is a further aspect of these proposals which ought to be considered, namely, the manner in which the cash flow of co-operatives will be affected. What is envisaged here will completely destroy the operation of the co-ops; it will make it impossible for them to carry on their operations within the structure they have developed over the years. There is one alternative open to them: they can simply change over to a stock company type of operation. But if they did that they would be abandoning the principles upon which the movement has developed and flourished. Consider the question of shares. A share, as we speak of it in the co-op movement, is a completely different thing from a share in an ordinary corporate operation.
It should be kept in mind that the only source of equity capital for co-ops is through the patronage refund system as they have developed it. Again, they could reorganize on a different basis, but if they did they would no longer be co-operatives; they would no longer be carrying on as in the past. The bill will make it impossible for them to operate as they desire to operate, and this is a serious matter.
Similarly, it should be kept in mind that there is no means whereby credit can be obtained for corporate taxes paid under the new proposals before us. There is no dividend tax credit applied to pay-outs of patronage refunds as is available to recipients of dividends from ordinary stock corporations. This, too, is a discriminatory feature in the bill, one which is totally intolerable.
The co-operative movement has also pointed out that the new tax proposals will make it virtually impossible for most co-operatives even to consider paying dividends to their members. I hope the government will reconsider its proposals in this area, bearing in mind that the purpose of a co-op is not so much the earning of profit as the provision of services to those who have organized it.
I suggest that if the government allows clauses 135 to 137 to pass without substantial change and without giving substantial weight to the representations of the co-operative and credit union movements, it will destroy something that is essential to the future well-being of Canadian society. That is a cross that I am sure even a Liberal government would not want to have hanging around its neck.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this very important Bill C-259 because I feel the amendment moved by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) expresses very well the concern which is felt by a great many Canadians. The amendment reads: That this House deeply concerned with unacceptable levels of inflation, persisting unemployment and stagnant industry and conscious of the necessity for meaningful tax reform declines to give second reading to a bill which does not provide sufficient stimulus to the economy of Canada with appropriate tax cuts and incentives, does not contain adequate tax exemptions and is not calculated to materially improve business and labour conditions in Canada now or in the foreseeable future.
That expresses a concern which is felt by thinking Canadians generally at this time, particularly those who have studied this so-called tax reform bill. Taxation is an increasingly important factor in the economic life of our country. We have a situation in which we have two phenomena, which used to be considered to be mutually exclusive, occurring at the same time. The first is inflation and the other is high unemployment. It was once thought that you only had inflation in a period when the economy was buoyant and everybody was employed, and that you only had unemployment when the economy was in a depressed condition, when prices were stable or falling and when the value of the dollar was not being inflated

but deflated and going up in value. At the present time we have these two phenomena, a high rate of unemployment and a high rate of inflation, happening concurrently. A good question is, what new factor is there in the equation which makes this not only possible but perhaps inevitable?
In what I am about to say I will do my best to avoid being unduly partisan, because what I say is not criticism of this government only but criticism of our general outlook in government. It applies not only to this government but, in a larger context, perhaps to all levels of government. I believe our rate of increasing taxation has to be controlled. We tend to look at this progression of increase as so much of a percentage each year and it does not seem very serious. It may be just an increase of 10 per cent, or something of that sort, and we forget that it is a geometric progression. It is like the population explosion or compound interest rates: when they continue for a while the absolute increase is frightening and ultimately explosive.
I think I can illustrate what I am saying by a classic story which has various forms and settings. It is about a farmer who sent his hired boy to the blacksmith's shop to get a horse shod. As you will know, Mr. Speaker, there are 32 nails in a set of horseshoes. The regular charge for this job was $2. The blacksmith asked the boy whether he would prefer to be charged the $2, or would he like to be charged one cent for the first nail, twice as much for the next, twice as much for the next, and so on. The boy thought that there being only 32 nails, this would not be a very large amount. The blacksmith then pointed out that this was a compounding, or a geometric progression and that by doubling even 32 times you arrive at a colossal figure. As a matter of fact, I believe it would cost something like $21 million to have a horse shod on that basis. This is the kind of lack of appreciation for trends taking place in this and many countries which produces exponential curves which become steeper and steeper. They are trends which cannot continue becoming steeper and steeper with ever-increasing acceleration without something flying apart at the end.
Some people might say, "We have inflation, but what does that matter? If a dollar will only buy half as much now as it did X' number of years ago, it comes out to the same thing." It does not come out to the same thing. Inflation has a very great number of unfortunate effects on the economy. The first is that it discourages thrift and saving, because if one saves for the future, his old age or anything of that sort, the value of the savings is depreciated as the value of money goes down and inflation increases. The people who want to borrow money realize that the thing to do is not to have their property value in dollars but, rather, to have those dollars invested in perhaps stocks or real property.
The effect of this is that there are more people who want to borrow money than there are people willing to lend money. The people who lend money not only wish to have a reasonable rental on the money they loan, but also an increment on the interest which will neutralize the depreciation of the money in the period it is loaned. They do not want to lend a dollar with which one could buy a dollar's worth of goods and find that when they get that

Income Tax Act
dollar back a year from now it will only buy 95 cents worth of goods in terms of its original value. The result is high interest rates. That is an inevitable result of inflation. This places an added burden on people who invest in the means of production whether they be farmers, representatives of companies or anything else. They must borrow money, and while it is depreciated on their income tax return they are gypped because the depreciation they receive is in respect of cheap money.
When these people have to replace the capital goods and means of production at the end of that period, they find the replacement cost is twice what it had been. I will give an example, Mr. Speaker. This is a homey example. This summer I found it necessary to put a new roof on my barn. I am a farmer. The barn had been built many years ago and I happened to have the contractor's receipt from the time when this fair-sized building was built before the turn of the century. When I repaired the roof this year I found that the cost of just the nails to put on the roof was about the same as the cost of the whole building when it was first built. That is inflation.
We are experiencing a type of inflation which is becoming steeper all the time. It is very dangerous. I remember being appalled when I was told that when the Palace Hotel in Brussels was redecorated after World War II the inside decorations cost more than the total cost of the building just before World War I. I thought at that time, "Thank God we have not been exposed to that kind of inflation in North America". Now, however, we have that kind of inflation, or something very close to it. This concerns me greatly.
This situation makes it impossible for industry or business to plan for the future or to engage in many of the economic stimulations they could carry on if they were dealing with a dollar that was fairly constant. It would be an impossible task to try to plan for business expansion or for the future in a situation where the value of the dollar is wildly fluctuating, where you have wild inflation or where you have a rapid rate of inflation, because the businessman or the entrepeneur is in the same position as an engineer if he were called upon to plan a building like the Arts Centre and was told that his yardstick would expand by 5 per cent per year.
It is this type of difficulty which is slowing down our economy. Our economy is being slowed down by high taxes. One might say, of course, "We are paying high taxes, but governments are in so many fields of endeavour now and are giving good service in return for the tax dollars. We have many things such as the old age pension, medicare and better schooling." This is all good; it is excellent. I am for this so long as we can afford it and so long as we do not live beyond our means.
If we should find that we are living beyond our means we must make the difficult decision as to what our priorities are, because I believe our tax burden is already too heavy and that our tax load has been expanding at a rate which is much greater than the rate of expansion of either our population or our gross national product. This cannot go on idenfinitely. I would give an illustration or two about what I have in mind. I have here a statement which was prepared in reply to an answer to a question placed on the order paper last year. We find, for example, that the ratio of federal government employees to the population has increased, from 1950 to the present time, from one civil servant to 106 members of the population to one civil servant for every 87 members of the population.
In reply to another question we find, in absolute terms, that the number of civil servants in the federal civil service increased between 1934 and 1968 from 40,000 to 235,000. Yet in that period the population only doubled. I am not against civil servants. We have an excellent civil service in this country, comprised of dedicated people; but I believe it is unfair to them if it is government policy to expand government services to the extent that we have civil servants working in many non-productive fields.
As I have said, the effect of taxation on the Canadian economy is fairly extreme. I should like to quote some figures in respect of the total revenue of the federal government. I have the figures for only the period 1926 to 1946 and to 1966. The total revenue of the federal government increased from $373 million in 1926 to $2,602 million in 1946 and to $9,721 million in 1966. The municipal and provincial rates of revenue increased in roughly the same proportion, so that the total tax paid by Canadians to all three levels of government in a matter of 40 years has increased from a total of $879 million to $22,155 million in 1966, and the trend has continued. The fact that disturbs me is that this trend continues at an ever-increasing rate in most cases.
What is the end result of such a trend? To give an illustration of the end result, the taxes paid in Canada in the 40 years-per individual, per capita, not per wage earner-prior to 1966 increased from $87.90 to $1,107.75, to all levels of government. If the average family consists of four people, that is a tax burden of $4,400. It is no wonder that it is an absolute necessity, especially in the cities, for there to be at least two wage earners in a family so that they can make both ends meet. If there is not, their income does not allow them to own a home.
This sort of change in our economy affects the quality of life and the kind of homes that we are able to provide for our growing children. I think that from this situation stem some of the other problems that are facing Canada. One might suggest that big corporations can be taxed more, or that the sales tax can be increased since nobody knows whether the increase is part of the actual cost of production or not, and what the taxpayer does not know will not hurt him. So we keep on piling these hidden taxes on everyone and there is no escape. I do not care whether a taxpayer's income is high or low, he pays through the nose day in and day out to all three levels of government. There is no escape for him, and the taxes that are imposed on corporations or on the so-called rich filter down through all income groups.
Let me give another illustration of the effect of high taxes. I have here a statement which I suppose all telephone subscribers received recently with their bill. It points out that the total tax on the Bell Canada telephone service, which must inevitably be paid by their customers whether the taxes are direct, indirect or merely collected by Bell and remitted to government, amounted to about $44 for each telephone in service last year. They write: Consider that we have more than six million phones in service and you'll see why we say we deal in "huge" numbers.
Income Tax Act

September 29, 1971
The tax per phone has increased by 90 per cent since 1960. This rate of increase in taxes is four times the rate of increase in general operating costs over the same decade.
This is a typical example of how high taxes affect business, because one cannot do much business now unless one has a telephone, at least one. But with one telephone you will be stuck with $44 worth of taxes which you have to pass on to your customers.
Automotive transportation I think is considered a business necessity for the transportation of goods. What happens at present? For example, from 1955 to 1970 the oil companies got three cents less for each gallon of gasoline that they produced than they did 15 years ago. The filling station operators who distribute the gasoline receive about the same as they did 15 years ago. Federal taxes have gone up by more than half a cent per gallon in that time, and other taxes have gone up by 6 cents a gallon, with the result that now, although the industry is so efficient that the costs of production and distribution have not increased in that period, the cost of a gallon of gasoline, which is an essential element of production, has gone up sharply.
I could go on, but I want to make the point that high taxes have an inhibiting effect on industry, and when I say industry I mean business in general down to a person who is self-employed. It is harder and harder for Canadians to compete in world markets or to continue in a business which might have been prosperous under similar
circumstances if the tax load were not as high. We cannot avoid taxing the means of production, and this is very unfortunate because it makes us uncompetitive in world markets.
We still feel that we live in an affluent society and should have the newest cars and everything we need. But how do we pay for this if we do not export competitively in world markets goods that have a high element of employment, that create many jobs? We are doing it less and less successfully. We are blessed with a tremendous hoard of natural resources, so we export them. They take a minimum of work and that keeps international payments in balance. But the result is that the Canadian dollar is relatively higher, compared with other currencies, than it would be if it were a measure of our competitiveness as it should be. This vicious circle makes it more difficult for us to compete in world markets, as the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans) pointed out so clearly the other day. The kind of life we are living as Canadians can be compared to the life of a farmer who could not make ends meet and decided to pay the grocery bill by selling some of his acreage every year.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
